newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Protest, apathy seen hurting Austria Euro-poll.
newsitem.headline: Protest, apathy seen hurting Austria Euro-poll.

text.p: Austrians voted on Sunday in their first elections for the European parliament with turnout looking well below figures for past national polls, reflecting possible anti-EU protests or simply voter apathy.

The election is the first popularity test of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's government since a general election last year and the introduction of a two-year austerity budget in March cutting welfare benefits and raising taxes.

With European Union membership being blamed by many for the country's ills, pollsters said voters could use the occasion to record their anger against the coalition government, and Vranitzky's Social Democrats in particular.

The far-right Freedom Party which campaigned against the Maastricht treaty on EU integration was hoping to increase its support to around 25 percent. Any higher figure would be regarded as a huge triumph for nationalist leader Joerg Haider.
The turnout in Austria's westernmost province Vorarlberg, where voting was completed by 4 p.m. (1400 GMT), was down to 58 percent from 83 percent in last December's general election.
Turnout in other constituencies around the country also showed signs of either voter apathy or an anti-EU abstention protest, with a drop of around 20 percent on last December.
Some 5.8 million voters are eligible to vote in the first Euro-poll held in Austria to fill the 21 seats allocated to the Alpine republic in the Strasbourg-based European Parliament.
Vienna state elections to determine the makeup of Austria's richest and most powerful province were also taking place.
The turnout in Vienna by 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) was down 13 percent compared to the general election.
Polling stations were due to close at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) when the first computer projections of the results were expected.
Many Austrians have blamed membership of the European Union over the past 22 months for record bankrupties, a series of company takeovers by foreign firms and rising unemployment.

Haider has accused the coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party of bungling Austria's entry into the EU and demands the renegotiation of net annual payments to Brussels of around 15 billion schillings ($1.5 billion).
The Social Democrats saw their support dip in one opinion poll to 31 percent, the lowest level since democratic elections were first held in Austria in 1918, and down from 38 percent last December.
Support dipping below 30 percent could spell disaster for the Social Democrats and might shake the federal government.
The People's Party, led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, has held steady in polls at around 28 percent.

The "feel-bad" factor could also have repercussions in the Vienna state election. Opinion polls have suggested Vranitzky's Social Democrats could lose their majority control of the capital for the first time since 1945.
The Social Democrats, who have used Vienna as its policy showcase for half a century, may be forced to rule the city in coalition with the conservatives or the leftist Green Party.
